There's a particular hour — not quite night, no longer evening — when the house settles into itself. The refrigerator hums its one note. A car passes, and its headlights draw a slow white parallelogram across the ceiling, then leave. In that light's wake the room seems darker than before, as if it had only been borrowing brightness and now had to give it back.

I think most of life happens in hours like this. Not the graduations or the emergencies, not the moments we photograph, but the unwitnessed stretches when nothing is happening and therefore everything is. The mind, denied an event, begins making its own: old conversations replayed with better endings, hypothetical arguments won decisively, faces of people we haven't thought about in fifteen years surfacing with perfect clarity and no context.

We treat these hours as filler, as the space between the real parts. But I've started to suspect the opposite — that this is the actual substance, and the marked occasions are just the punctuation. A life is mostly the hum of the refrigerator. Mostly the walk to the car. Mostly the particular quality of light at 4 p.m. in October, which no one will ever describe accurately to anyone.

Maybe that's why we keep things we don't need: a ticket stub, a chipped mug, a jacket that no longer fits. They're not souvenirs of events at all. They're proof of the unphotographed hours, quiet witnesses to the long middle of a life, which is to say the life itself.
